Good-humored, relaxed, and carefree, he ran his whale-boat as if the deadliest encounter were just a dinner party and his crew all invited guests. He was as fussy about arranging his end of the boat comfortably as an old stagecoach driver is about how snug his seat is. When close up to the whale, in the very death-lock of the fight, he handled his merciless lance coolly and casually, the way a whistling tinker handles his hammer. He would hum his old rigadig tunes while side by side with the most furious monster. For this Stubb, long habit had turned the jaws of death into an easy chair. What he thought about death itself, nobody can say. Whether he ever thought about it at all might be a fair question; but if he ever did happen to turn his mind that way after a comfortable dinner, then no doubt, like a good sailor, he took it as a kind of call of the watch to tumble up aloft and get busy there with something he would find out about when he obeyed the order, and not before.

The name is my own invention, since there is more than one kind of porpoise, and something has to be done to tell them apart. I call him that because he always swims in hilarious schools, which keep flinging themselves skyward on the open sea like caps thrown up in a Fourth-of-July crowd. Sailors usually greet their appearance with delight. Brimming with high spirits, they always come from the breezy waves to windward. They are the lads who always live before the wind. They're thought to be a lucky sign. If you yourself can keep from giving three cheers at the sight of these lively fish, then heaven help you; you haven't got the spirit of godly playfulness in you. items.new: On one of those southern whalers, on a long voyage of three or four years, as often happens, the hours you spend at the masthead add up to several whole months. And it's a great pity that the place where you spend so large a share of your entire natural life should be so sadly lacking in anything like cozy homeliness, or anything suited to breeding a comfortable sense of belonging to a spot, such as goes with a bed, a hammock, a hearse, a sentry box, a pulpit, a coach, or any of those other small, snug contraptions in which men shut themselves away for a time. Your usual perch is the top of the topgallant mast, where you stand on two thin parallel sticks (almost unique to whalemen) called the topgallant crosstrees. Up there, tossed about by the sea, the beginner feels roughly as cozy as he would standing on a bull's horns. Of course, in cold weather you can take your house aloft with you in the form of a watch-coat; but strictly speaking, the thickest watch-coat is no more a house than your bare body is. For just as the soul is glued inside its fleshly tabernacle, and can't move around freely in it, or even move out of it, without great risk of perishing (like an ignorant pilgrim crossing the snowy Alps in winter), so a watch-coat is not so much a house as a mere envelope, or an extra skin wrapped around you. You can't put a shelf or a chest of drawers inside your body, and neither can you make a handy closet out of your watch-coat.
